I have a friend who lives in a building that used to be a library. Not the kind with a new wing and a coffee shop and a quiet floor where people wear headphones and pretend to study. This one is the real thing, the kind that smells like paper and dust and the faint metallic tang of old radiators. The city tore down half the block for condos, but the library survived because the foundation was bad and it was cheaper to leave it than to move it. So now it sits half in shadow, with a chain-link fence around it and a sign that says CITY PROPERTY - DO NOT ENTER.

He lives there anyway. He has a key he got from a former janitor who owed him a favor. He says the key doesn't work on the front doors anymore but he goes in through the loading dock where the metal has warped enough that a grown man can slip through. Once inside, he pushes books back onto shelves, turns off the alarms that still buzz faintly in the basement, and lives in the space between the stacks.

He doesn't read for pleasure, at least not anymore. He reads for inventory. He knows which shelves have been stripped by scavengers and which still hold their weight. He knows the Dewey numbers by the feel of the spines under his fingertips. He knows that the 813.54 section still smells like mildew and that the 398 section, folklore, has a pigeon nest in the top corner that he feeds every morning with crumbs of stale bread.

The thing he does that I keep thinking about is that he writes letters. Every day, for about three hours, he sits at a long oak table that the librarians used for reference and writes letters to people who will never read them. He has a stack of library cards he found in a box in the basement, hundreds of them, yellowed and bent, each with a name and an address that is almost certainly wrong now. Some of the cards are from 1978, some from 1994. One is from 1962. He writes to all of them.

He writes to Mrs. Eleanor Vance, 1428 Maple Ave, who checked out "The Complete Works of Jane Austen" on March 14, 1987, and never returned it. He writes: Dear Mrs. Vance, I hope you are well. I was thinking about you today because I found your card. I imagine you kept the books, or perhaps you lent them to someone and lost track. Either way, I hope you read them. I hope Emma made you laugh. 

He writes to a boy named Marcus Chen, who checked out a comic book in 2003. He writes about what Marcus might be doing now, about whether he still draws. He writes to a woman named Rosa Delgado who checked out cookbooks for fifteen straight years. He writes recipes back to her.

He tells me he doesn't send them. He just writes them and puts them in a cardboard box under the table. The box is full. The box is overflowing. He has a second box now. He says the letters are not for the people on the cards. They're for the building.

I didn't understand that until he took me there last winter. It was January and the heat was off and my breath made clouds. The windows were boarded but light came in through cracks and made the dust visible. It was beautiful in a way that felt illegal. The stacks went up in dark corridors, and every corridor ended in something different: a reading room with chairs overturned, a children's section with plastic animals half buried in debris, a periodical room where the magazines were stacked like geological layers.

He showed me his apartment, which was really just the old librarian's office. He had a mattress on the floor, a hot plate, a kettle, a small solar lamp. On the walls he had taped up the letters. Hundreds of them, covering every inch. The handwriting was his, neat and small, filling the pages with looping sentences. It was like living inside someone's diary.

"Why do you do it?" I asked.

He shrugged. "Someone has to remember them. The library remembers everyone who ever came in. The computer logs are gone. The card catalog is gone. The city doesn't care. But the building does. It holds the shape of people. The letters are just me listening."

I think about that a lot when I'm on the train. About how cities are full of buildings that remember things people don't. The library holds the ghost of Mrs. Vance reading Austen in a quiet corner in 1987. It holds the ghost of the boy who checked out a comic and ran out the door with it under his arm. It holds the librarian who reshelved books for forty years and knew everyone's name. All of that is still there, in the way the light hits a certain aisle at 4 pm, in the smell of the paper, in the way the floor creaks in a particular spot.

We talk about memory as if it's inside us. It's not only inside us. It's in the places we leave marks. A coffee stain on a table. A worn spot on a stair. A library card that never got returned. The building is an archive of attention. People paid attention there. They chose books. They sat down. They waited for a phone call. They read to their children. They hid from rain. All of that attention is still suspended in the walls.

My friend is not a writer. He says he can't write a story to save his life. He can only write letters. And maybe that's the point. A letter is an act of faith. You write to someone you think might still be there, somewhere. You don't need them to answer. You just need to believe that the address is real enough to hold your words for a while.

He also collects things. Not valuable things. He collects the small detritus of reading. A bookmark made from a receipt. A paperclip bent into a heart. A child's drawing left in a book. A pressed flower between the pages of a botany text. He puts them in jars. The jars line his windowsill. He calls it his museum of small attentions.

I asked him once if he was lonely. He said no, that loneliness is a different thing. He said he is accompanied. The building talks back. The pigeons talk. The letters talk. He said the hardest part is leaving. When he goes to buy food, he feels like he's abandoning a conversation.

Sometimes I think about the ethics of it. He's trespassing. He's living in a condemned building. If he gets hurt, if the building falls, who's responsible? But then I think about how many buildings we let die because they're inconvenient. How many libraries we close because attendance is down. How many stories we throw away because they don't make money. My friend is a squatter, yes, but he's also a caretaker. He keeps the place from being completely erased. He keeps the lights on, metaphorically. He feeds the pigeons. He writes the letters.

I wonder what would happen if the city ever actually cleaned it out. If they sent crews to clear it. What would they find? A man, a mattress, a hot plate, two cardboard boxes full of letters to strangers. Would they think it's sad? Would they think it's beautiful? Would they understand that the letters were never really about the people on the library cards, but about the idea that someone once cared enough to check out a book?

He told me about one letter he wrote that he did send. He found an address that looked current, a woman named Helen Park who had checked out a book on birdwatching in 1991. He looked her up, found a phone number, called, asked if she was the same Helen Park. She was. She was eighty-three. She remembered the library. She remembered the book. She said she had moved three times since then and had lost track of half her life. She cried when he read her the letter he had written. She said it was the first time in years someone had written to her without wanting something.

He cried too. He told me that night. He said he realized the letters were not just for the building. They were for the living, too. We are all archives. We are all full of half-returned books.

I have started writing letters myself, though not to strangers. I write to my younger self, to people I lost, to my mother who is still here. I write them and I keep them in a drawer. Sometimes I read them. Sometimes I don't. It doesn't matter. The act of writing them makes the air in my apartment feel different, like someone is listening.

My friend still lives in the library. I go see him once a month. He makes tea. We sit at the reference table and he shows me new letters. The handwriting gets tighter as the winter gets colder. He says the building is settling. He says he can hear it at night, the old wood and plaster shifting. He says it's like the building is breathing.

I think about how we are all living in buildings that remember us, and how we are all building places inside ourselves that will remember us after we are gone. A sentence you read at twelve. A song you heard on a bus. The smell of your grandmother's kitchen. All of that is a library.

If you ever find yourself in a city that has an old library that's been closed, go look at it. Don't break in. Just look at it from the street. Look at the windows, the boarded doors, the way the light hits it at dusk. Imagine the people who were there. Imagine the books they touched. Imagine the letters they never wrote.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe memory doesn't need to be perfect. Maybe it just needs someone to sit at a table and pay attention for a while, to write a letter to a stranger and believe that the words matter even if no one reads them.

My friend says the building will fall eventually. The city will come. He will have to leave. He says when that day comes, he will take the letters with him. He will find a new building. He will start again.

I asked him if he ever wants to write a novel. He laughed. "Novels are about one person. This is about everyone."

And I think that's the most honest thing anyone has ever said to me about writing. It's not about making something new. It's about remembering what was already there, and giving it a little more time to exist.

So I write now, not because I have something to say, but because I want to make sure someone is listening. I write to you, stranger, reading this on a screen somewhere, in a room that smells like your own particular life. I don't know your name. I don't know your address. But I imagine you. I imagine you reading this and thinking about a place you used to go. I hope you have a place like that. I hope you remember it kindly.

If you don't, build one. Sit down at a table. Write a letter to someone. It doesn't matter who. It only matters that you write as if the building is listening. Because it is.

The dust in the air is made of all the words we have ever read. The light through the cracks is made of all the attention we have ever paid. The letters in the box under the table are made of all the love we have not yet learned how to give.

And that, I think, is enough to live for. That, and feeding the pigeons every morning.
